div.head: Early English Laws and Legal Language
div.p: eLiebermann is a digital edition and research resource for the laws of early England, from the code of Æthelberht of Kent (c. 600) to the Anglo-Norman law books of the twelfth century. Its foundation is Felix Liebermann’s Die Gesetze der Angelsachsen (1903–16), still the standard edition of the laws, whose texts, translation, dictionary and apparatus it makes searchable, linked and readable in English. Around Liebermann it gathers the editions, translations and scholarship of the century since, so that a law, the words it uses, and what scholars have said about both can be studied together.

The project is edited by Anya Adair (The University of Hong Kong) and was supported by the Research Grants Council of Hong Kong (General Research Fund 17604022). It is in public beta: material is added and corrected continuously, and readers’ corrections are welcome through the button for suggesting a change on every dictionary entry and clause. The editorial principles are set out under Editorial Principles; the project, its people and how to cite it are described under About.

The laws clause by clause, in Liebermann’s divisions and in his order: the Old English, Latin or French text as he prints it, labelled by manuscript; his German translation, with an English rendering of it; the texts and translations of later editors; and Liebermann’s textual notes and commentary. Each clause is indexed by subject, and linked to the clauses that Liebermann and later scholars compare with it, so that a provision can be followed from code to code. Two Latin translations that Liebermann prints only in pieces, the Instituta Cnuti and the Consiliatio Cnuti, can also be read as continuous texts.

A digital edition of Liebermann’s Wörterbuch (Gesetze II.1), the dictionary of the Old English, Latin and French words of the laws. His abbreviations, grammatical terms and sigla are expanded and translated on the page; every clause he cites is linked to the clause itself, with the word marked; and headwords are linked to Bosworth–Toller and the Dictionary of Old English, a work still being checked.

Liebermann’s apparatus, expanded and translated: his sigla for the law codes and manuscripts, with his descriptions of the manuscripts; his grammatical terms and abbreviations; the authors and works he cites; his own account of how to read the dictionary; and his forewords, in German and in English.
